//: Art spec for `node tools/genimage.js`. One entry per figure being re-rendered in the house semi-realistic style. Each prompt says only what the picture must DEPICT — the standing requirements (semi-realistic register, Zambian setting, gender balance, a visible disability wherever people appear, no lettering) are appended to every prompt by the tool, so they are deliberately absent here. Learners in this book are Form 2: about 14 to 16 years old.
//answer-bearing: image20 and image21 are NOT listed, and must never be regenerated. Both sit inside the END OF TOPIC ASSESSMENT for Topic 2.1, directly under 'Study the map below and answer questions that follow', and the answers are read off the artwork itself. image20 carries the grid map behind ten questions — the four-figure reference for the village, the six-figure reference for the police station and the post office, what feature sits at 115222, where the District Commissioner's office is, and the bearing of the DC office from the post office. image21 carries the contour island behind eight more — the height of A, the altitude of K, the landforms at F, G and H, the distance L to M, and the gradient of slope D. A generated replacement would place every one of those features somewhere else, so every printed answer would become wrong while still looking plausible. image20's real defect is photographic, not pictorial (it is a skewed camera photo of a book page with a black border and page curl), and the fix for that is to deskew and de-border the picture that is already there, keeping the data exactly where it is.
//lettering: image4 ('Figure 1: Major map Symbols') is not listed either. It is a topographic map KEY, which means its content is almost entirely lettering — about forty symbol/label pairs, in English with a French subtitle under each. The tool appends 'no lettering' to every prompt by design, so a generated version could only come back as unlabelled symbol artwork with the whole key still to be set as type. That is a typesetting job, not a generation job: the honest options are to typeset the key as a real two-column figure or to keep the upscaled scan. Left out until that is decided.
//resolution: Generated at 1536px on the long edge and then taken through Real-ESRGAN (4x, resampled back down) by the tool, because the model's own output is short of CLAUDE.md's 300 DPI at the size these print. A topic-opener picture prints across 142mm of text width, which needs 1677px; the 1800px default clears it.

image22.jpeg.//: The opening illustration for TOPIC 2.2 BASIC RESEARCH SKILLS. It carries no caption and nothing in the text depends on its detail, so it can be redrawn freely. The original is a generated photograph whose flipchart is covered in garbled machine lettering — 'Access TO Clean Water INcome Attsunces', 'High participation in community meetings:' — which is legible enough at print size to read as nonsense. The replacement keeps exactly what the original depicted: learners presenting fieldwork findings back to the community they surveyed. The chart is asked for BLANK, with its bars and pie clearly drawn but no words, so the figure shows real research work without any lettering for the model to mangle.
image22.jpeg.prompt: Outdoors in a Zambian village under a broad shade tree, four secondary school learners of about fifteen in school uniform present their fieldwork findings to a seated group of village elders and children. A large paper flipchart stands on a wooden easel facing the audience, and on it are a clearly drawn bar chart of four coloured bars and a pie chart divided into three coloured wedges — the charts drawn cleanly and confidently, but carrying absolutely no words, numbers, titles or labels of any kind, and no ruled lines standing in for writing. One learner stands beside the easel with an arm raised toward the pie chart, mid-explanation; two others hold clipboards and pencils; a fourth, a boy who uses a wheelchair, sits at the front of the group of presenters with papers on his lap, turned in and taking part. Two boys and two girls among the learners. Seated on low benches and on the ground in front of them, six villagers of mixed ages — an older man in a wide-brimmed hat, two women in bright chitenge print with headwraps, an older man in a cap, and two small children — listening and looking at the chart. Thatched and brick houses with rust-coloured roofs behind, green hills in the far distance, dry grass, warm late-afternoon light. The mood is proud, attentive and friendly.
